claim: Time-resolved X-ray diffraction of isolated fast-twitch muscles of mice was used to show how structural changes in the myosin-containing thick filaments contribute to the regulation of muscle contraction.
source: Time-resolved X-ray diffraction of isolated fast-twitch muscles of mice was used to show how structural changes in the myosin-containing thick filaments contribute to the regulation of muscle contraction, extending the previous focus on regulation by the actin-containing thin filaments.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the experimental approach and findings of the study.

claim: Muscle activation involves thin filament activation, disruption of the helical array of myosin motors, release of myosin motor domains from the folded conformation, and actin attachment in sequence.
source: This study shows that muscle activation involves the following sequence of structural changes: thin filament activation, disruption of the helical array of myosin motors characteristic of resting muscle, release of myosin motor domains from the folded conformation on the filament backbone, and actin attachment.
evidence: The abstract describes the sequential structural changes observed during muscle activation based on the X-ray diffraction data.

claim: Physiological force generation in the twitch response is limited by incomplete activation of the thick filament and rapid inactivation of both filaments.
source: Physiological force generation in the 'twitch' response of skeletal muscle to single action potential stimulation is limited by incomplete activation of the thick filament and the rapid inactivation of both filaments.
evidence: The abstract states the mechanisms limiting force generation in the twitch based on the study's findings.

claim: Muscle relaxation after repetitive stimulation is accompanied by complete recovery of the folded motor conformation but incomplete reformation of the helical array.
source: Muscle relaxation after repetitive stimulation is accompanied by a complete recovery of the folded motor conformation on the filament backbone but by incomplete reformation of the helical array, revealing a structural basis for post-tetanic potentiation in isolated muscles.
evidence: The abstract describes the structural changes observed during relaxation after tetanic stimulation.

claim: The incomplete reformation of the helical array after tetanic stimulation provides a structural basis for post-tetanic potentiation.
source: Muscle relaxation after repetitive stimulation is accompanied by a complete recovery of the folded motor conformation on the filament backbone but by incomplete reformation of the helical array, revealing a structural basis for post-tetanic potentiation in isolated muscles.
evidence: The abstract explicitly links the incomplete recovery of helical array structure to post-tetanic potentiation.

claim: The twitch is triggered by a transient increase in intracellular calcium concentration.
source: The unitary contractile response of skeletal muscle to an action potential in the muscle cell membrane—the twitch—is triggered by a transient increase in intracellular calcium concentration ([Ca2+]i), leading to calcium binding to troponin in the actin-containing thin filaments.
evidence: The introduction describes the established mechanism of twitch initiation.

claim: Calcium binding to troponin initiates a change in thin filament structure where tropomyosin moves from its blocking position, allowing myosin heads to bind to actin and generate force.
source: This, in turn, initiates a change in the thin filament structure in which tropomyosin moves from its blocking position in resting muscle, allowing myosin head or motor domains from the thick filaments to bind to actin and generate force (Gordon et al., 2000).
evidence: The introduction describes the established mechanism of thin filament activation with citation support.

claim: Peak [Ca2+]i is an order of magnitude larger than the dissociation constant of the Ca2+ regulatory sites on troponin.
source: The duration of the [Ca2+]i transient is much briefer than the mechanical response in the twitch, but peak [Ca2+]i is an order of magnitude larger than the dissociation constant of the Ca2+ regulatory sites on troponin, which become fully occupied with a delay of less than 1 ms after peak [Ca2+]i in mammalian muscle at 28°C (Baylor and Hollingworth, 2003).
evidence: The introduction cites published data on calcium concentration and troponin binding kinetics.

claim: Ca2+ regulatory sites on troponin become fully occupied with a delay of less than 1 ms after peak [Ca2+]i in mammalian muscle at 28°C.
source: The duration of the [Ca2+]i transient is much briefer than the mechanical response in the twitch, but peak [Ca2+]i is an order of magnitude larger than the dissociation constant of the Ca2+ regulatory sites on troponin, which become fully occupied with a delay of less than 1 ms after peak [Ca2+]i in mammalian muscle at 28°C (Baylor and Hollingworth, 2003).
evidence: The introduction cites published data on troponin calcium binding kinetics.

claim: The movement of tropomyosin in the thin filament has a half-time of about 5 ms in amphibian fast-twitch muscles at 22°C.
source: The movement of tropomyosin in the thin filament is also much faster than force development, with a half-time of about 5 ms as determined by time-resolved X-ray diffraction in amphibian fast-twitch muscles at 22°C, conditions in which the twitch duration is about 100 ms (Kress et al., 1986).
evidence: The introduction cites published X-ray diffraction data on tropomyosin movement kinetics.

claim: Peak force in the twitch is much less than that produced at full activation during a tetanus.
source: Although the thin filaments are rapidly and fully activated in the twitch, the peak force in the twitch is much less than that produced at full activation, as produced in intact muscles by repetitive high-frequency stimulation in a tetanus.
evidence: The introduction describes the well-established difference in force production between twitch and tetanus.

claim: The force at the tetanus plateau is about four times larger than that at the peak of the twitch in mammalian fast-twitch muscles at near-physiological temperature.
source: The force at the tetanus plateau is about four times larger than that at the peak of the twitch in mammalian fast-twitch muscles at near-physiological temperature.
evidence: The introduction provides a quantitative comparison of twitch and tetanus force.

claim: Tetanic stimulation increases the duration, but not the peak amplitude, of the [Ca2+]i transient compared to that in the twitch.
source: Tetanic stimulation increases the duration, but not the peak amplitude, of the [Ca2+]i transient or the peak occupancy of the Ca2+ regulatory sites on troponin compared to that in the twitch (Baylor and Hollingworth, 2003).
evidence: The introduction cites published data on calcium transients during tetanic stimulation.

claim: The [Ca2+]i transient provides a 'start' signal for contraction but does not control either the amplitude or the time course of the twitch in skeletal muscle.
source: It follows that the [Ca2+]i transient provides a 'start' signal for contraction but does not control either the amplitude or the time course of the twitch in skeletal muscle.
evidence: The introduction draws an inference from the cited calcium transient data.

claim: The rate of force development is effectively limited by the rate of binding of myosin motors to thin filaments.
source: The rate of force development is effectively limited by the rate of binding of myosin motors to thin filaments, as determined from the time course of instantaneous stiffness during force development in tetani of amphibian muscle at 4°C after taking filament compliances into account (Brunello et al., 2006; Fusi et al., 2014a).
evidence: The introduction cites published mechanical studies on the rate-limiting step of force development.

claim: In resting muscle, myosin motors are folded back against the filament backbone in a helical array stabilised by interactions with other myosin motors and other thick filament components, including myosin-binding protein-C (MyBP-C) and titin.
source: In resting muscle, the myosin motors are not available to interact with actin and generate contraction because they are folded back against the filament backbone in a helical array stabilised by interactions with other myosin motors and other thick filament components, including myosin-binding protein-C (MyBP-C) and titin (Irving, 2017; Woodhead et al., 2005).
evidence: The introduction describes the structural state of myosin motors in resting muscle with citation support.

claim: The thick filament 'off' state minimises ATP hydrolysis and the associated whole-body metabolic cost in resting muscle.
source: This thick filament 'off' state, sometimes described as the 'super-relaxed' state, minimises ATP hydrolysis and the associated whole-body metabolic cost in resting muscle (Stewart et al., 2010), but its existence raises the question of how the thick filament, which does not appear to have a direct calcium signalling mechanism, is activated by electrical stimulation.
evidence: The introduction cites published work on the metabolic function of the thick filament off state.

claim: The thick filament can be directly activated by mechanical stress.
source: Part of the answer to that question was provided by the discovery that the thick filament can be directly activated by mechanical stress (Fusi et al., 2016; Linari et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites published work on mechanical activation of thick filaments.

claim: Switching on the thick filaments is faster than force development in amphibian muscle at 4°C.
source: More generally, X-ray studies of the rising phase of the tetanus in amphibian muscle at 4°C showed that switching on the thick filaments is faster than force development (Reconditi et al., 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites published X-ray studies on thick filament activation kinetics.

claim: Relaxation can be separated into a slow, almost linear phase ('isometric relaxation') followed by rapid 'chaotic relaxation' in isolated myofibrils and single fibres from amphibian muscle.
source: In isolated myofibrils and in single fibres from amphibian muscle, relaxation can be clearly separated into a slow, almost linear phase in which sarcomere lengths remain almost constant ('isometric relaxation') followed by mechanical yielding and rapid 'chaotic relaxation' in which the remaining force is rapidly lost (Brunello et al., 2009; Poggesi et al., 2005).
evidence: The introduction cites published work on the phases of muscle relaxation.

claim: All measurements on mouse EDL muscle were made at 28°C.
source: All of the present measurements on mouse EDL muscle were made at 28°C, a temperature at which the muscles contract reproducibly as required for signal averaging in X-ray experiments.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the experimental temperature.

claim: The time course of the [Ca2+]i transient and its binding to troponin has been characterised in mouse EDL at 28°C.
source: Moreover, the time course of the [Ca2+]i transient and its binding to troponin has been characterised in mouse EDL at 28°C (Baylor and Hollingworth, 2003), and the peak force is very close to that at the mammalian body temperature (Caremani et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites published characterization of calcium dynamics at the experimental temperature.

claim: The peak force in mouse EDL at 28°C is very close to that at mammalian body temperature.
source: Moreover, the time course of the [Ca2+]i transient and its binding to troponin has been characterised in mouse EDL at 28°C (Baylor and Hollingworth, 2003), and the peak force is very close to that at the mammalian body temperature (Caremani et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites published data on force production at different temperatures.

claim: The off structure of the thick filament is preserved in mammalian muscle at 28°C.
source: Most importantly, the off structure of the thick filament is preserved in mammalian muscle at this temperature (Caremani et al., 2021), in contrast with nearly all the published studies of thin filament regulation, for example, those using pCa titrations with steady-state Ca buffering in skinned muscle fibres, which were made at a relatively low temperature in order to minimise the irreversible effects of sustained high levels of activation at a high temperature.
evidence: The introduction cites published work showing preservation of thick filament structure at the experimental temperature.

claim: Five sarcomere reflections were observed, corresponding to even orders of the sarcomere repeat from the 10th to the 18th order in resting muscle.
source: Five sarcomere reflections were observed, corresponding to even orders of the sarcomere repeat from the 10th to the 18th order in resting muscle (Figure 1A,B, cyan) (Bordas et al., 1987; Reconditi et al., 2014).
evidence: The results section describes the observed X-ray reflections with reference to the figure and citations.

claim: Sarcomere length in the resting muscles was about 2.4 µm.
source: Sarcomere length in the resting muscles was about 2.4 µm (Figure 1D; Table 1).
evidence: The results section reports the measured sarcomere length with reference to figure and table.

claim: Sarcomere length in the tetanus reached a roughly constant value of 2.13 µm from about 20 ms after the first stimulus.
source: The sarcomere reflections became much weaker during stimulation, but sarcomere length in the tetanus reached a roughly constant value of 2.13 µm from about 20 ms after the first stimulus (Figure 1D, filled circles; Table 1), indicating that the sarcomeres in the central region of the muscle from which the X-ray signals were recorded had shortened by about 12%, presumably by stretching the tendons or compliant regions at the ends of the muscle fibres.
evidence: The results section reports the measured sarcomere length during tetanus with reference to figure and table.

claim: Sarcomeres in the central region of the muscle shortened by about 12% during tetanus.
source: The sarcomere reflections became much weaker during stimulation, but sarcomere length in the tetanus reached a roughly constant value of 2.13 µm from about 20 ms after the first stimulus (Figure 1D, filled circles; Table 1), indicating that the sarcomeres in the central region of the muscle from which the X-ray signals were recorded had shortened by about 12%, presumably by stretching the tendons or compliant regions at the ends of the muscle fibres.
evidence: The results section calculates the sarcomere shortening from the measured lengths.

claim: Sarcomere length was maintained for about 20 ms after the last stimulus while force decreased to about 80% of its plateau value.
source: This sarcomere length was maintained for about 20 ms after the last stimulus while force decreased to about 80% of its plateau value (Figure 1C,D, filled circles).
evidence: The results section describes the temporal relationship between sarcomere length and force during relaxation.

claim: Relaxation of mouse EDL muscle from 100-ms tetani exhibits clear 'isometric' and 'chaotic' phases similar to those described previously in isolated myofibrils and single fibres from amphibian muscle.
source: Relaxation of mouse EDL muscle from 100-ms tetani, therefore, exhibits clear 'isometric' and 'chaotic' phases similar to those described previously in isolated myofibrils and single fibres from amphibian muscle (Brunello et al., 2009; Poggesi et al., 2005).
evidence: The results section compares the observed relaxation phases to previously published findings.

claim: There appeared to be little sarcomere shortening in the twitch.
source: There appeared to be little sarcomere shortening in the twitch (Figure 1D, open circles), although the very low intensity of the sarcomere reflections (Figure 1E, open circles) suggests that sarcomere lengths became inhomogeneous, as during the first 20 ms of the tetanus.
evidence: The results section describes the sarcomere behavior during twitch with reference to figures.

claim: The (1,0) reflection became much weaker on activation in both the tetanus and the twitch, signalling motion of the myosin motors away from the thick filament backbone.
source: The (1,0) reflection became much weaker on activation in both the tetanus (Figure 2A, orange) and the twitch (Figure 2B), signalling motion of the myosin motors away from the thick filament backbone (Haselgrove and Huxley, 1973).
evidence: The results section describes the observed change in X-ray reflection with citation support for interpretation.

claim: The (1,1) reflection became broader on activation and its integrated intensity increased, signalling increased mass at the trigonal positions of the filament lattice occupied by the thin filaments and increased disorder.
source: The (1,1) reflection became broader on activation and its integrated intensity increased (Figure 2A,B, orange), signalling not only increased mass at the trigonal positions of the filament lattice occupied by the thin filaments, but also increased disorder.
evidence: The results section describes the observed change in X-ray reflection and its structural interpretation.

claim: I1,1/I1,0 was ~0.4 at rest and ~1.8 at the tetanus plateau.
source: I1,1/I1,0 was ~0.4 at rest and ~1.8 at the tetanus plateau, similar to values reported previously for mouse EDL (Caremani et al., 2019), and ~0.9 at the peak of the twitch (Table 1).
evidence: The results section reports the measured intensity ratios with citation to previous work.

claim: I1,1/I1,0 was ~0.9 at the peak of the twitch.
source: I1,1/I1,0 was ~0.4 at rest and ~1.8 at the tetanus plateau, similar to values reported previously for mouse EDL (Caremani et al., 2019), and ~0.9 at the peak of the twitch (Table 1).
evidence: The results section reports the measured intensity ratio at twitch peak force.

claim: The increase in I1,1/I1,0 was faster than force development at the start of the tetanus.
source: The increase in I1,1/I1,0 was faster than force development at the start of the tetanus (Figure 2C, filled circles; Table 2), as observed in single fibres from amphibian fast skeletal muscle (Cecchi et al., 1991).
evidence: The results section describes the temporal relationship between X-ray signal and force with citation to previous work.

claim: Myosin motors move towards the thin filaments before they bind strongly to actin or generate force.
source: Since the fraction of myosin motors strongly attached to actin has the same time course as force (Brunello et al., 2006), the faster change in I1,1/I1,0 shows that myosin motors move towards the thin filaments before they bind strongly to actin or generate force.
evidence: The results section draws an inference from the temporal relationship between X-ray signal and force with citation support.

claim: IAL1 increased by a factor of almost three in the tetanus with a time course similar to that of force development.
source: IAL1 increased by a factor of almost three in the tetanus (Figure 3C) with a time course similar to that of force development, but recovered faster than force during isometric and chaotic relaxation, showing that myosin motors detach from actin in both phases.
evidence: The results section describes the observed change in actin layer line intensity and its temporal relationship to force.

claim: IAL1 recovered faster than force during isometric and chaotic relaxation, showing that myosin motors detach from actin in both phases.
source: IAL1 increased by a factor of almost three in the tetanus (Figure 3C) with a time course similar to that of force development, but recovered faster than force during isometric and chaotic relaxation, showing that myosin motors detach from actin in both phases.
evidence: The results section draws an inference about motor detachment from the temporal relationship between X-ray signal and force.

claim: The intensity of the first myosin layer line (IML1) decreased following the start of stimulation with a time course much faster than that of force development.
source: The intensity of the first myosin layer line (IML1) decreased following the start of stimulation (Figure 3D) with a time course much faster than that of force development, showing that the loss of folded helical conformation of myosin motors on activation is much faster than their attachment to actin (Figure 3D; Table 2).
evidence: The results section describes the observed change in myosin layer line intensity and draws an inference about motor conformation.

claim: The loss of folded helical conformation of myosin motors on activation is much faster than their attachment to actin.
source: The intensity of the first myosin layer line (IML1) decreased following the start of stimulation (Figure 3D) with a time course much faster than that of force development, showing that the loss of folded helical conformation of myosin motors on activation is much faster than their attachment to actin (Figure 3D; Table 2).
evidence: The results section draws an inference about the sequence of structural changes from the temporal relationship between X-ray signals.

claim: IML1 decreased almost as much at the peak of the twitch as at the plateau of the tetanus.
source: Consistent with this faster response, IML1 decreased almost as much at the peak of the twitch (Figure 3D, open circles; Table 1) as at the plateau of the tetanus (filled circles).
evidence: The results section compares the magnitude of IML1 decrease in twitch and tetanus.

claim: IML1 did not recover during isometric relaxation after tetanic stimulation, consistent with myosin motors not reforming the folded helical conformation in this phase.
source: IML1 did not recover during isometric relaxation after tetanic stimulation (Figure 3D, filled circles), consistent with the above conclusion that myosin motors do not reform the folded helical conformation in this phase, despite the fall of force and detachment of myosin motors from actin.
evidence: The results section describes the observed lack of IML1 recovery and draws an inference about motor conformation.

claim: IML1 recovered rapidly but incompletely during chaotic relaxation; the 'off' conformation of the myosin motors had not been recovered even 120 ms after the last stimulus.
source: IML1 recovered rapidly but incompletely during chaotic relaxation; the 'off' conformation of the myosin motors characteristic of the resting state had not been recovered even 120 ms after the last stimulus.
evidence: The results section describes the incomplete recovery of IML1 during chaotic relaxation.

claim: The M6 reflection is associated with a periodic structure in the thick filament backbone with an axial repeat of ~7.2 nm.
source: The M6 reflection is associated with a periodic structure in the thick filament backbone with an axial repeat of ~7.2 nm (Reconditi et al., 2004; Huxley et al., 2006).
evidence: The results section describes the structural origin of the M6 reflection with citation support.

claim: SM6 increased by 1.54 ± 0.02% at the peak of the tetanus.
source: The intensity of M6 reflection (IM6) was roughly constant during activation, within the reproducibility of the data (Figure 4C), but its spacing (SM6) increased consistently by 1.54 ± 0.02% at the peak of the tetanus (Figure 4D, filled circles; Table 1), and by 0.95 ± 0.04% at the peak of the twitch (open circles).
evidence: The results section reports the measured change in M6 spacing during tetanus.

claim: SM6 increased by 0.95 ± 0.04% at the peak of the twitch.
source: The intensity of M6 reflection (IM6) was roughly constant during activation, within the reproducibility of the data (Figure 4C), but its spacing (SM6) increased consistently by 1.54 ± 0.02% at the peak of the tetanus (Figure 4D, filled circles; Table 1), and by 0.95 ± 0.04% at the peak of the twitch (open circles).
evidence: The results section reports the measured change in M6 spacing during twitch.

claim: The spacing increase in SM6 is associated with activation of the thick filament.
source: This spacing increase is associated with activation of the thick filament (Haselgrove, 1975).
evidence: The results section cites published work linking SM6 spacing increase to thick filament activation.

claim: SM6 increased much faster than force at the start of the tetanus.
source: SM6 increased much faster than force at the start of the tetanus (Table 2).
evidence: The results section describes the temporal relationship between SM6 and force development.

claim: SM6 recovered with the same time course as force during isometric relaxation.
source: Following the last stimulus, SM6 recovered with the same time course as force during isometric relaxation, but more slowly during chaotic relaxation (Figure 4D, filled circles).
evidence: The results section describes the temporal relationship between SM6 and force during relaxation.

claim: SM6 recovery was still incomplete more than 120 ms after the last stimulus.
source: SM6 recovery was still incomplete more than 120 ms after the last stimulus, and there was a smaller recovery deficit following a twitch.
evidence: The results section describes the incomplete recovery of SM6 after tetanus.

claim: The M3 reflection is associated with the axial periodicity of the myosin motors along the thick filaments.
source: The M3 reflection is associated with the axial periodicity of the myosin motors along the thick filaments and has been used extensively to obtain information about the conformation and motion of myosin motors during activation, force generation, and relaxation (Brunello et al., 2009; Brunello et al., 2006; Reconditi et al., 2011; Reconditi et al., 2004).
evidence: The results section describes the structural origin of the M3 reflection with citation support.

claim: IM3 decreased transiently in the tetanus before becoming about three times larger than at rest at the tetanus plateau.
source: The intensity of the M3 reflection (IM3) decreased transiently in the tetanus before becoming about three times larger than at rest at the tetanus plateau (Figure 5C, filled circles; Table 1).
evidence: The results section describes the biphasic change in IM3 during tetanus.

claim: The initial decrease in IM3 may be partly due to the loss of some of the helically folded myosin motors and partly due to destructive interference between the actin-attached and folded populations of motors.
source: The initial decrease may be partly due to the loss of some of the helically folded myosin motors that were present in the resting muscle and partly due to the destructive interference between the actin-attached and folded populations of motors (Reconditi et al., 2011).
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation of the initial IM3 decrease with citation support.

claim: The slower increase in IM3 is associated with formation of actin-attached force-generating motors that have their long axes more perpendicular to the filament axis.
source: The slower increase is associated with formation of actin-attached force-generating motors that have their long axes more perpendicular to the filament axis.
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation of the IM3 increase during tetanus.

claim: IM3 only decreased in the twitch.
source: IM3 only decreased in the twitch (open circles).
evidence: The results section describes the different behavior of IM3 in twitch compared to tetanus.

claim: SM3 increased by 1.36 ± 0.01% at the tetanus plateau.
source: The spacing of the M3 reflection (SM3) increased by 1.36 ± 0.01% at the tetanus plateau and by 0.57 ± 0.05% at the peak of the twitch (Figure 5D, Table 1), slightly smaller than the corresponding percentage increases in SM6 described above.
evidence: The results section reports the measured change in M3 spacing during tetanus.

claim: SM3 increased by 0.57 ± 0.05% at the peak of the twitch.
source: The spacing of the M3 reflection (SM3) increased by 1.36 ± 0.01% at the tetanus plateau and by 0.57 ± 0.05% at the peak of the twitch (Figure 5D, Table 1), slightly smaller than the corresponding percentage increases in SM6 described above.
evidence: The results section reports the measured change in M3 spacing during twitch.

claim: The increase in SM3 during the rising phase of the tetanus was faster than force but slower than SM6.
source: The increase in SM3 during the rising phase of the tetanus was faster than force but slower than SM6 (Table 2).
evidence: The results section describes the temporal relationship between SM3, force, and SM6.

claim: SM3 remained remarkably constant during isometric relaxation.
source: SM3 remained remarkably constant during isometric relaxation (Figure 5D, filled circles), although IM3 recovered substantially towards its resting value (Figure 5C), indicating that the motors that detach from actin during isometric relaxation become disordered.
evidence: The results section describes the behavior of SM3 during isometric relaxation and draws an inference about motor disorder.

claim: The motors that detach from actin during isometric relaxation become disordered.
source: SM3 remained remarkably constant during isometric relaxation (Figure 5D, filled circles), although IM3 recovered substantially towards its resting value (Figure 5C), indicating that the motors that detach from actin during isometric relaxation become disordered.
evidence: The results section draws an inference about motor disorder from the different behaviors of SM3 and IM3.

claim: SM3 decreased rapidly at the onset of chaotic relaxation and had completely recovered to its resting value at the end of mechanical relaxation.
source: SM3 decreased rapidly at the onset of chaotic relaxation and had completely recovered to its resting value at the end of mechanical relaxation.
evidence: The results section describes the recovery of SM3 during chaotic relaxation.

claim: A new peak (the 'star' peak) appeared transiently on the LA side of the M3 reflection about 10 ms after the start of stimulation.
source: Unexpectedly, a new peak appeared transiently on the LA side of the M3 reflection about 10 ms after the start of stimulation (Figure 5A,B, green), with a spacing of 14.832 ± 0.013 nm during the tetanus rise (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, green triangle) and 14.878 ± 0.018 nm at the peak of the twitch (orange triangle).
evidence: The results section describes the observation of a transient peak in the M3 reflection.

claim: The star peak had a spacing of 14.832 ± 0.013 nm during the tetanus rise.
source: Unexpectedly, a new peak appeared transiently on the LA side of the M3 reflection about 10 ms after the start of stimulation (Figure 5A,B, green), with a spacing of 14.832 ± 0.013 nm during the tetanus rise (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, green triangle) and 14.878 ± 0.018 nm at the peak of the twitch (orange triangle).
evidence: The results section reports the measured spacing of the star peak during tetanus.

claim: The star peak had a spacing of 14.878 ± 0.018 nm at the peak of the twitch.
source: Unexpectedly, a new peak appeared transiently on the LA side of the M3 reflection about 10 ms after the start of stimulation (Figure 5A,B, green), with a spacing of 14.832 ± 0.013 nm during the tetanus rise (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, green triangle) and 14.878 ± 0.018 nm at the peak of the twitch (orange triangle).
evidence: The results section reports the measured spacing of the star peak during twitch.

claim: A peak with a similar spacing to the star peak was seen previously on cooling of resting EDL muscle of mice and demembranated fibres from rabbit psoas muscle.
source: A peak with a similar spacing was seen previously on cooling of resting EDL muscle of mice and demembranated fibres from rabbit psoas muscle (Caremani et al., 2021; Caremani et al., 2019), an intervention that mimics activation of the thick filament.
evidence: The results section cites previous observations of a similar peak under different conditions.

claim: The best-fit model parameters were similar at rest and following mechanical relaxation after a twitch or tetanus.
source: As expected from the similarity of the experimental M3 profiles, the best-fit model parameters were similar at rest and following mechanical relaxation after a twitch or tetanus (Figure 6B,E,G; Table 3).
evidence: The results section describes the similarity of model parameters across different conditions.

claim: At rest, nm was 2 and nd close to 46, indicating that nearly all 49 layers of myosin motors were ordered.
source: nm was 2 and nd close to 46, indicating that nearly all 49 layers of myosin motors were ordered, with the likely exception of three layers at the filament tips.
evidence: The results section interprets the model parameters in terms of the number of ordered motor layers.

claim: At the tetanus plateau, all layers were ordered; nm was 1 and nd was 49.
source: At the tetanus plateau (Figure 6F), all layers were ordered; nm was 1 and nd was 49.
evidence: The results section reports the model parameters at tetanus plateau.

claim: At the peak of the twitch, only myosin motors in a central region of each half-filament were ordered.
source: nd was slightly smaller during early activation and at the peak of the twitch (Figure 6C,D), and nm was larger at the peak of the twitch, indicating that only myosin motors in a central region of each half-filament were ordered (Figure 6A), though that region did not correspond to either the conventional 'C-zone' defined by the presence of MyBP-C (green) or the 'C-type' titin repeats (magenta) (Bennett et al., 2020; Caremani et al., 2021; Tonino et al., 2019).
evidence: The results section interprets the model parameters at twitch peak force in terms of the spatial distribution of ordered motors.

claim: The average movement of the centre of mass of the myosin motors away from the M line on activation was 11 nm.
source: The average movement of the centre of mass of the myosin motors away from the M line on activation was 11 nm, the same as in the present experiments (Table 3).
evidence: The results section reports the calculated movement of motor center of mass.

claim: There was no significant axial motion of the myosin heads during early activation.
source: However, the best-fit hbz values in Table 3 also show that there was no significant axial motion of the myosin heads during early activation, reflecting the similarity of the intensity of the LA peak at this time point (Figure 5A,E, green; Figure 6C) to that at rest (Figure 5A,E, cyan; Figure 6B) and in marked contrast to the large reduction of the helical order of the myosin heads during early activation signalled by IML1 (Figure 3D, green).
evidence: The results section draws an inference about motor motion from the model parameters and X-ray data.

claim: The helical order is lost before myosin motors are released from the folded conformation on the filament backbone.
source: Moreover, in the early activation time-frame, centred at 6.5 ms after the stimulus, IML1 had reduced by 50% (Figure 3D, green), but there was no axial movement of the centre of mass of the myosin motors (hbz, Table 3), strongly suggesting that the helical order of the myosin motors is lost before their release from the folded conformation on the filament backbone.
evidence: The discussion section draws an inference about the sequence of structural changes from the X-ray data.

claim: At the peak of the twitch, hbz had moved by about 6 nm, about half-way to its tetanus plateau value, suggesting that a significant fraction of motors remain in the folded state in the twitch.
source: At the peak of the twitch, hbz had moved by about 6 nm, about half-way to its tetanus plateau value, suggesting that a significant fraction of motors remain in the folded state in the twitch.
evidence: The results section draws an inference about the fraction of folded motors in the twitch from the model parameters.

claim: The changes in thick filament structure during the tetanus can be correlated with force changes in five sequential phases: activation, tetanus plateau, isometric relaxation, chaotic relaxation, and mechanically relaxed.
source: The functional significance of these structural changes is clearer for tetanus than for twitch, in which activation and relaxation are clearly separated by a period of steady-state sarcomere-isometric contraction in which the thin filaments are maximally activated by calcium. Changes in thick filament structure during the tetanus can be correlated with force changes in five sequential phases, which we refer to as activation, tetanus plateau, isometric relaxation, chaotic relaxation, and mechanically relaxed, where the latter is distinct from the resting state achieved several minutes after a previous contraction.
evidence: The discussion section describes the framework for interpreting the structural changes.

claim: The changes in the thick-filament-based X-ray reflections in the five phases are qualitatively similar to those described previously in fast-twitch amphibian muscles.
source: Where analogous protocols have been employed, the changes in the thick-filament-based X-ray reflections in these five phases are qualitatively similar to those described previously in fast-twitch amphibian muscles, as described below.
evidence: The discussion section compares the present findings to previous work on amphibian muscle.

claim: The fastest changes in thick filament structure during activation are the loss of the helical order of the myosin motors and the elongation of the filament backbone.
source: The fastest changes in thick filament structure during activation are the loss of the helical order of the myosin motors, signalled by the ML1 reflection, and the elongation of the filament backbone, signalled by SM6.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the fastest structural changes during activation.

claim: The half-time for the loss of the helical order of the myosin motors during the tetanus rise was about 8 ms.
source: The fraction of molecules in a given conformation is proportional to the amplitude (A) of an X-ray reflection, the square root of its intensity. Therefore, the half-time for the loss of the helical order of the myosin motors during the tetanus rise was estimated from the change in AML1, which has a half-time of about 8 ms, the same as that of SM6 (Table 2).
evidence: The discussion section reports the calculated half-time for loss of helical order.

claim: The half-time of SM6 change during tetanus rise was about 8 ms.
source: The fraction of molecules in a given conformation is proportional to the amplitude (A) of an X-ray reflection, the square root of its intensity. Therefore, the half-time for the loss of the helical order of the myosin motors during the tetanus rise was estimated from the change in AML1, which has a half-time of about 8 ms, the same as that of SM6 (Table 2).
evidence: The discussion section reports the half-time for SM6 change.

claim: The equatorial intensity ratio (I1,1/I1,0), the fractional intensity of the LA peak of the M3 reflection (LM3), and the axial spacing of the myosin motors (SM3) have half-times of about 11 ms.
source: A second group of signals, including the equatorial intensity ratio (I1,1/I1,0), the fractional intensity of the LA peak of the M3 reflection (LM3), and the axial spacing of the myosin motors (SM3), have half-times that are slightly slower, about 11 ms.
evidence: The discussion section reports the half-times for a second group of structural signals.

claim: The change in the spacing of the filament backbone (SM6) is synchronous with the loss of helical order of the motors.
source: At the time resolution of these experiments, the change in the spacing of the filament backbone (SM6) is synchronous with the loss of helical order of the motors, whereas the axial periodicity of the motors (SM3) and their radial motion (I1,1/I1,0) are synchronous with the loss of the folded population.
evidence: The discussion section describes the temporal relationships between different structural changes.

claim: The axial periodicity of the motors (SM3) and their radial motion (I1,1/I1,0) are synchronous with the loss of the folded population.
source: At the time resolution of these experiments, the change in the spacing of the filament backbone (SM6) is synchronous with the loss of helical order of the motors, whereas the axial periodicity of the motors (SM3) and their radial motion (I1,1/I1,0) are synchronous with the loss of the folded population.
evidence: The discussion section describes the temporal relationships between different structural changes.

claim: The amplitude of the first actin layer line (AAL1) has a half-time of 15 ms, similar to that of force.
source: The amplitude of the first actin layer line (AAL1), signalling myosin motor binding to the thin filaments, has a half-time of 15 ms, similar to that of force.
evidence: The discussion section reports the half-time for AAL1 change and compares it to force development.

claim: AM3 has a half-time of 21 ms, slower than force.
source: The only X-ray signal that is slower than force is AM3 (half-time, 21 ms), and this is likely related to its biphasic response (Figure 5C), with a fast decreasing phase followed by a slower rising phase.
evidence: The discussion section reports the half-time for AM3 change and provides an interpretation.

claim: This sequence of structural changes during activation is similar to that reported for single fast-twitch fibres from frog skeletal muscle at 4°C, although all the changes are about three times faster in the conditions of the present experiments.
source: This sequence of structural changes during activation is similar to that reported for single fast-twitch fibres from frog skeletal muscle at 4°C (Brunello et al., 2006; Piazzesi et al., 1999; Reconditi et al., 2011), although all the changes are about three times faster in the conditions of the present experiments.
evidence: The discussion section compares the present findings to previous work on frog muscle.

claim: The fastest structural changes in the thick filaments are slower than calcium activation of the thin filaments.
source: The fastest structural changes in the thick filaments, those reported by AML1 and SM6, are slower than calcium activation of the thin filaments.
evidence: The discussion section compares the kinetics of thick and thin filament activation.

claim: The peak of the intracellular [Ca2+] transient is only 2.0 ms after the stimulus in mouse EDL muscle at 28°C.
source: The peak of the intracellular [Ca2+] transient is only 2.0 ms after the stimulus in mouse EDL muscle at 28°C, and Ca2+ binding to troponin lags this by less than 1 ms (Baylor and Hollingworth, 2003).
evidence: The discussion section cites published data on calcium transient kinetics.

claim: The rate of calcium-binding to troponin in response to a [Ca2+] jump is greater than 1000 s−1 at 12°C in demembranated fibres from rabbit psoas muscle.
source: Fluorescent probes on troponin in demembranated fibres from rabbit psoas muscle showed that the rate of calcium-binding in response to a [Ca2+] jump is greater than 1000 s−1 at 12°C (Fusi et al., 2014b).
evidence: The discussion section cites published data on calcium binding kinetics.

claim: In frog sartorius muscle at 22°C, the half-time of the increase in AAL2 was less than 4 ms, about twice as fast as the change in AML1 in those conditions.
source: In frog sartorius muscle at 22°C, the half-time of the increase in AAL2 was less than 4 ms, about twice as fast as the change in AML1 in those conditions (Kress et al., 1986).
evidence: The discussion section cites published data on thin filament activation kinetics.

claim: Activation of the thick filaments in fast-twitch skeletal muscle has two structural components with time courses intermediate between those of thin filament activation and attachment of myosin motors to actin.
source: Activation of the thick filaments in fast-twitch skeletal muscle, therefore, has two structural components with time courses intermediate between those of thin filament activation and attachment of myosin motors to actin.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the temporal sequence of structural changes during activation.

claim: The delay between thick filament activation and actin attachment is thought to be the result of a structural or biochemical transition in the myosin head in which its catalytic domain becomes strongly bound to actin in a state capable of generating force or filament sliding.
source: The delay between thick filament activation and actin attachment is thought to be the result of a structural or biochemical transition in the myosin head in which its catalytic domain becomes strongly bound to actin in a state capable of generating force or filament sliding (Brenner and Eisenberg, 1987; Goldman, 1987).
evidence: The discussion section cites published hypotheses about the mechanism of the delay between thick filament activation and actin attachment.

claim: The thin filaments are fully activated at the tetanus plateau, and about 30% of the myosin motors are likely to be strongly attached to actin.
source: The thin filaments are fully activated at the tetanus plateau, and about 30% of the myosin motors are likely to be strongly attached to actin (Caremani et al., 2019; Linari et al., 2007).
evidence: The discussion section cites published estimates of the fraction of actin-attached motors at tetanus plateau.

claim: The average movement of the centre of mass of the myosin motors between the resting state and the tetanus plateau was 11 nm, the same as that reported previously for single fibres from amphibian muscle.
source: Modelling the axial profile of the M3 reflection (Figure 6; Table 3) showed that the average movement of the centre of mass of the myosin motors between the resting state and the tetanus plateau was 11 nm, the same as that reported previously for single fibres from amphibian muscle (Reconditi et al., 2011), in which the conformation of the motors at the tetanus plateau had been determined by perturbation experiments using length or load steps (Irving et al., 2000; Piazzesi et al., 2007; Piazzesi et al., 2002).
evidence: The discussion section compares the calculated motor movement to previous work on amphibian muscle.

claim: The conformation of both the actin-bound myosin motors at the tetanus plateau and their helical folded conformation in resting muscle is likely the same in amphibians and mammals.
source: Given the similarity of sarcomere structure and filament protein isoforms in the two muscle types, it seems very likely that the conformation of both the actin-bound myosin motors at the tetanus plateau and their helical folded conformation in resting muscle is the same in amphibians and mammals.
evidence: The discussion section draws an inference about the conservation of motor conformations across species.

claim: Isometric relaxation was first characterised in single fibres from amphibian muscle as a relatively slow, almost linear phase of force decline to about half the tetanus plateau value at a constant sarcomere length after the end of stimulation.
source: Isometric relaxation was first characterised in single fibres from amphibian muscle as a relatively slow, almost linear phase of force decline to about half the tetanus plateau value at a constant sarcomere length after the end of stimulation (Brunello et al., 2009; Edman and Flitney, 1982).
evidence: The discussion section cites previous characterization of isometric relaxation.

claim: The rate of isometric relaxation is not limited by the rate of removal of calcium from the intracellular solution but by the isometric rate of detachment of myosin motors from actin.
source: Subsequent studies on isolated myofibrils showed that the rate of isometric relaxation is not limited by the rate of removal of calcium from the intracellular solution but by the isometric rate of detachment of myosin motors from actin (Poggesi et al., 2005).
evidence: The discussion section cites published work on the rate-limiting step of isometric relaxation.

claim: The initial rate of dissociation of calcium from troponin following electrical stimulation is fast and has been estimated as about 200 s−1 in mouse EDL at 28°C.
source: In intact muscle fibres, the initial rate of dissociation of calcium from troponin following electrical stimulation is fast (Caputo et al., 1994; Konishi, 1998) and has been estimated as about 200 s−1 in mouse EDL at 28°C (Baylor and Hollingworth, 2003).
evidence: The discussion section cites published estimates of calcium dissociation kinetics.

claim: Mouse EDL muscles do not show a clear linear phase or 'shoulder' in the time course of mechanical relaxation.
source: Mouse EDL muscles do not show a clear linear phase or 'shoulder' in the time course of mechanical relaxation (Figure 1C), and a sarcomere-isometric phase of relaxation has not been reported previously to our knowledge, probably because it is difficult to measure the sarcomere length in these muscles by diffraction of visible light.
evidence: The discussion section describes the observed relaxation behavior in mouse EDL.

claim: Sarcomeres in mouse EDL muscle remain precisely isometric for the first ~20 ms after the last stimulus while force decays to about 80% of its plateau value.
source: However, ultra-low-angle X-ray diffraction (Figure 1) shows that sarcomeres in mouse EDL muscle do remain precisely isometric for the first ~20 ms after the last stimulus (Figure 1C), while force decays to about 80% of its plateau value at a progressively increasing rate.
evidence: The discussion section describes the sarcomere-isometric phase of relaxation observed by X-ray diffraction.

claim: I1,1/I1,0 and IAL1 decrease during isometric relaxation, signalling detachment of myosin motors from thin filaments.
source: I1,1/I1,0 and IAL1 decrease during isometric relaxation, signalling detachment of myosin motors from thin filaments.
evidence: The discussion section interprets the X-ray signals during isometric relaxation.

claim: X-ray signals related to the regulatory state of the thick filament, including IML1, I1,0, and SM3, and the fractional intensities of the sub-peaks of the M3 reflection do not recover during isometric relaxation.
source: In contrast with the X-ray signals related to detachment of myosin motors from actin, those related to the regulatory state of the thick filament, including IML1, I1,0, and SM3, and the fractional intensities of the sub-peaks of the M3 reflection do not recover during isometric relaxation; there is no detectable recovery of the helical or folded motor conformations characteristic of resting muscle.
evidence: The discussion section describes the lack of recovery of thick filament structure during isometric relaxation.

claim: There is no detectable recovery of the helical or folded motor conformations during isometric relaxation.
source: In contrast with the X-ray signals related to detachment of myosin motors from actin, those related to the regulatory state of the thick filament, including IML1, I1,0, and SM3, and the fractional intensities of the sub-peaks of the M3 reflection do not recover during isometric relaxation; there is no detectable recovery of the helical or folded motor conformations characteristic of resting muscle.
evidence: The discussion section describes the lack of recovery of motor conformations during isometric relaxation.

claim: The delay between the loss of actin-attached myosin motors and the recovery of their ordered resting conformation means that there must be a transient population of disordered motors during isometric relaxation.
source: The delay between the loss of actin-attached myosin motors and the recovery of their ordered resting conformation means that there must be a transient population of disordered motors during isometric relaxation.
evidence: The discussion section draws an inference about the existence of disordered motors during isometric relaxation.

claim: The overall half-time of the detachment of myosin motors from actin during isometric and chaotic relaxation estimated from AAL1 is about 23 ms.
source: The overall half-time of the detachment of myosin motors from actin during isometric and chaotic relaxation estimated from AAL1, about 23 ms (Table 2), or from I1,1/I1,0 (30ms), is similar to that of mechanical relaxation itself (27 ms).
evidence: The discussion section reports the calculated half-time for motor detachment during relaxation.

claim: Recovery of the helical order of the motors during chaotic relaxation, as assessed by AML1, is slower, with a half-time of about 42 ms.
source: Recovery of the helical order of the motors during chaotic relaxation, as assessed by AML1, is slower, with a half-time of about 42 ms (Table 2), indicating a significant delay between motor detachment and reformation of the helically ordered resting state.
evidence: The discussion section reports the calculated half-time for recovery of helical order and draws an inference about the delay.

claim: The incomplete recovery of IML1 during mechanical relaxation shows that the helical order of the motors characteristic of resting muscle had not recovered when force was close to baseline.
source: The incomplete recovery of IML1 during mechanical relaxation shows that the helical order of the motors characteristic of resting muscle had not recovered when force was close to baseline (Figure 3).
evidence: The discussion section interprets the incomplete recovery of IML1.

claim: Only about 80% of motors had regained the helical conformation as estimated by AML1.
source: Only about 80% of motors had regained that conformation as estimated by AML1.
evidence: The discussion section estimates the fraction of motors that recovered the helical conformation.

claim: The axial profile of the M3 reflection and the inferred average centre of mass of the myosin motors had completely recovered at mechanical relaxation.
source: In contrast, the axial profile of the M3 reflection and the inferred average centre of mass of the myosin motors had completely recovered at mechanical relaxation (Figure 6G; Table 3), showing that the myosin motors had folded back against the filament backbone but had not fully reformed the resting helix.
evidence: The discussion section describes the complete recovery of motor folding but incomplete recovery of helical order.

claim: The myosin motors had folded back against the filament backbone but had not fully reformed the resting helix at mechanical relaxation.
source: In contrast, the axial profile of the M3 reflection and the inferred average centre of mass of the myosin motors had completely recovered at mechanical relaxation (Figure 6G; Table 3), showing that the myosin motors had folded back against the filament backbone but had not fully reformed the resting helix.
evidence: The discussion section draws an inference about the state of motors at mechanical relaxation.

claim: The incomplete recovery of helical packing of myosin motors after mechanical relaxation is likely to be the structural correlate of post-tetanic potentiation.
source: The incomplete recovery of helical packing of myosin motors after mechanical relaxation is likely to be the structural correlate of the enhanced twitch force observed after a tetanus, post-tetanic potentiation (Close et al., 1968).
evidence: The discussion section links the incomplete recovery of helical packing to post-tetanic potentiation with citation support.

claim: Myosin motors that have not returned to the helical array would be expected to be recruited more readily by a subsequent stimulus, leading to an enhanced twitch response.
source: Myosin motors that have not returned to the helical array would be expected to be recruited more readily by a subsequent stimulus, leading to an enhanced twitch response.
evidence: The discussion section provides a mechanistic explanation for post-tetanic potentiation.

claim: Peak force in a twitch is only about one-quarter of that produced during steady full activation at the tetanus plateau in mouse EDL muscle at 28°C.
source: Peak force in a twitch is only about one-quarter of that produced during steady full activation at the tetanus plateau in mouse EDL muscle at 28°C.
evidence: The discussion section reports the quantitative difference in force between twitch and tetanus.

claim: The lower force in the twitch is primarily due to the lower fraction of myosin motors attached to actin at the peak of the twitch, in comparison with the ~30% of motors attached at the tetanus plateau.
source: The X-ray data presented above show that this is primarily due to the lower fraction of myosin motors attached to actin at the peak of the twitch, in comparison with the ~30% of motors attached at the tetanus plateau (Caremani et al., 2019).
evidence: The discussion section draws an inference about the mechanism of lower twitch force from the X-ray data.

claim: The calcium regulatory sites on troponin in the thin filaments are likely to be fully occupied, albeit transiently, at the peak of the twitch.
source: Despite the low force and number of actin-attached motors, the calcium regulatory sites on troponin in the thin filaments are likely to be fully occupied, albeit transiently, at the peak of the twitch.
evidence: The discussion section draws an inference about troponin calcium occupancy during the twitch.

claim: Peak intracellular [Ca2+] is almost the same in the twitch and tetanus.
source: Peak intracellular [Ca2+] is almost the same in the twitch and tetanus, and calcium binding to troponin is fast (Baylor and Hollingworth, 2003).
evidence: The discussion section cites published data on calcium concentration in twitch and tetanus.

claim: Thick filaments are not fully activated at the peak of the twitch.
source: In contrast, thick filaments are not fully activated at the peak of the twitch.
evidence: The discussion section draws an inference about thick filament activation state during the twitch.

claim: Although the helical array of myosin motors has been disrupted at the peak of the twitch, a significant fraction of motors remain folded back onto the filament surface.
source: Although the helical array of myosin motors has been disrupted, as signalled by the decreased intensity of the ML1 layer line (Figure 3), a significant fraction of motors remain folded back onto the filament surface (Figure 6, Table 3), making them unavailable for binding to the activated thin filament.
evidence: The discussion section draws an inference about motor conformation during the twitch from the X-ray data.

claim: The low level of thick filament activation is at least partially responsible for the low fraction of actin-attached motors and force in the twitch.
source: The low level of thick filament activation is at least partially responsible for the low fraction of actin-attached motors and force in the twitch.
evidence: The discussion section draws an inference about the role of thick filament activation in limiting twitch force.

claim: The overall duration of the twitch is primarily determined by the brevity of thin filament activation.
source: Although the rate of force development in a twitch, like that in a tetanus, is limited by the rate of thick filament activation and actin attachment, the overall duration of the twitch is primarily determined by the brevity of thin filament activation.
evidence: The discussion section draws an inference about the determinants of twitch duration.

claim: The calcium transient has a half-time of only about 2 ms at 28°C.
source: The calcium transient has a half-time of only about 2 ms at 28°C.
evidence: The discussion section reports the half-time of the calcium transient.

claim: The half-time of Ca2+ dissociation from troponin is about 50 ms in mouse EDL at 16°C, likely corresponding to about 25 ms at 28°C.
source: The half-time of Ca2+ dissociation from troponin is about 50 ms in mouse EDL at 16°C (Baylor and Hollingworth, 2003), likely corresponding to about 25 ms at 28°C, close to the half-time of force relaxation in the twitch at this temperature (Table 2).
evidence: The discussion section cites published data and extrapolates to the experimental temperature.

claim: Thick filament inactivation in the twitch as monitored by the ML1 layer line has a half-time of about 29 ms, only slightly slower than force relaxation and thin filament inactivation.
source: Thick filament inactivation in the twitch as monitored by the ML1 layer line has a half-time of about 29 ms (Table 2), only slightly slower than force relaxation and thin filament inactivation as estimated above.
evidence: The discussion section reports the half-time for thick filament inactivation during twitch relaxation.

claim: In contrast with the delayed thick filament inactivation during isometric relaxation after a tetanus, thick and thin filament inactivation in twitch relaxation is almost synchronous.
source: Thus, in contrast with the delayed thick filament inactivation during isometric relaxation after a tetanus, thick and thin filament inactivation in twitch relaxation is almost synchronous.
evidence: The discussion section compares the kinetics of thick and thin filament inactivation in twitch versus tetanus relaxation.

claim: The force generated in the twitch is partly limited by the incomplete activation of the thick filament, although thin filament activation is transiently complete.
source: In summary, the force generated in the twitch—the unitary physiological response of skeletal muscle to action potential stimulation—is partly limited by the incomplete activation of the thick filament, although thin filament activation is transiently complete.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the mechanisms limiting twitch force.

claim: The rate of attachment of myosin motors to actin is partly limited by thick filament activation.
source: The rate of attachment of myosin motors to actin, resolved more clearly in the tetanus, is also partly limited by thick filament activation.
evidence: The discussion section draws an inference about the rate-limiting step of motor attachment.

claim: Thin and thick filament inactivation are rapid and synchronous within the time resolution of current data.
source: Thin and thick filament inactivation are rapid and synchronous within the time resolution of current data, and this also contributes to the low fraction of myosin motors attached to actin and peak force in the twitch.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the kinetics of filament inactivation during twitch relaxation.

claim: This dual-filament description of the regulation of muscle contraction extends the previous narrower focus on structural changes in the thin filament.
source: This dual-filament description of the regulation of muscle contraction extends the previous narrower focus on structural changes in the thin filament and establishes a physiological structural and functional framework for testing small molecules as potential therapeutics for muscle weakness.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the significance of the findings.
